gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a generator only does its job in a whole-home battery kit if its voltage and start wiring match the battery's hub. On the Anker SOLIX E10, a 120 V portable generator recharges at no more than 1,800 W (versus 7,680 W at 240 V). The Power Dock takes only 240 V generators. Anker's own AC Generator Adapter is listed as 240 V, 40 A and 'Currently not compatible with Power Dock'. Automatic start needs a 240 V generator with Two Wire or Utility Sensing control. Anker's Smart Generator 5500 avoids all of this through a dedicated 4,500 W DC cable, but The Solar Lab found it 'can only charge one stack at a time'.
standout_why: I compared against the four pages ChatGPT cited. The FranklinWH FAQ 'Can I use a generator with my FranklinWH system?' (both URLs) says portable and standby generators work, and its only quality advice reads 'low-quality inverter generators are recommended', which looks like a typo. The FranklinWH Generator Module page says it works with 'a range of both standby and portable generators' and gives no voltage, start-wire, kW or THD limits. The aPower 2 page only lists 'generator' as a charging source. None of them says that 120 V versus 240 V changes the recharge rate four-fold, that auto-start needs a 2-wire or utility-sensing generator, or that the adapter for third-party generators doesn't fit one of the two hubs. ChatGPT's answer itself says the capability 'should be confirmed before choosing equipment' but never says what to check. This finding decides the set: Power Dock plus Smart Generator 5500 (DC, auto-start), or Smart Inlet Box plus the AC Generator Adapter plus a 240 V generator. A 120 V portable generator is the wrong buy in either case.
kit_items: Battery and inverter: Anker SOLIX E10 (Power Module + B6000 battery). It is sold on ankersolix.com (rakuten:ankersolix), so the whole kit fills one cart. It charges at 7,680 W on 240 V but only 1,800 W on 120 V.
Transfer hub: Anker SOLIX Power Dock (200 A, 120/240 V split phase). Generator circuits 1–2 are rated 100 A max / 80 A continuous. Anker requires an installer trained on the Power Dock.

Generator: Anker SOLIX Smart Generator 5500 (tri-fuel). It connects through a dedicated 4,500 W DC cable that carries both power and control, so the system can start it automatically by battery level. That avoids the 240 V / two-wire / THD requirements a third-party AC generator would have to meet.

Don't add: the E10 AC Generator Adapter to a Power Dock kit. Anker lists it as 'Currently not compatible with Power Dock'. It only belongs in an E10 Standalone or Smart Inlet Box kit, with a 240 V generator.

findings.label: Stacks charged per generator
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX E10 Full System Review: True Home Backup? (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: The Solar Lab (no author or date shown; ©2026) says the generator 'can only charge one stack at a time'. Because solar and generator inputs connect to the inverters rather than the Power Dock, 'charging isn't evenly distributed across battery stacks'. This matters for Dealectric's listed 2× Power Module E10 kit. The review also says that without a Power Dock or Smart Inlet Box 'you're limited to basic 120V charging', which it calls 'extremely slow and not very practical'.

findings.label: Max charge rates per reviewer
findings.value: 1,800 W at 120 V, 9,600 W at 240 V, 4,500 W from Smart Generator
findings.source_title: A whole-house UPS beats buying UPS for every device, and the math is obvious (XDA, Joe Rice-Jones, 2026-06-22)
findings.note: Joe Rice-Jones of XDA tested a system with the Power Dock and Smart Generator, installed by Anker. He reports the generator 'will be automatically started by the system when needed' and supplies 'DC direct to the batteries'. He reported no generator faults, but had no solar connected.
